title: Pre-pour slab inspection
l1: A pre-pour inspection checks important construction work before concrete placement makes that work difficult or impossible to inspect.
l2: The relevant work is inspected before the concrete pour and any identified issues are addressed before proceeding.
l3: The required checks depend on the work present at the stage and the applicable project requirements.
l4: An experienced practitioner looks for work that will become concealed by the concrete and therefore needs to be checked before the pour.
l5: This activity depends on relevant pre-pour work being complete and occurs before concrete placement.

title: Temporary wall frame bracing
l1: Temporary bracing supports a wall frame while the structure is not yet fully stabilised by later construction work.
l2: Bracing is installed as part of the framing sequence and remains in place while temporary stability is required.
l3: The need and arrangement of temporary bracing depend on the frame condition and construction sequence.
l4: An experienced practitioner considers whether the partially completed frame can remain stable while subsequent work is carried out.
l5: Temporary bracing is connected to the wall framing sequence and later stability of the structure.

title: Wall frame inspection before concealment
l1: Wall framing should be inspected at an appropriate stage before later construction work conceals relevant parts of the frame.
l2: The frame is reviewed before subsequent lining or other work makes the relevant construction difficult to inspect.
l3: The timing of the inspection depends on when the relevant framing work will become concealed.
l4: An experienced practitioner pays particular attention to items that will no longer be visible after the next construction stage.
l5: The inspection depends on completion of the relevant framing work and precedes work that conceals the frame.

title: Roof framing set-out
l1: Roof framing set-out establishes the intended positions of roof framing elements before installation proceeds.
l2: Relevant positions are established and checked as part of the roof framing sequence before the associated members are installed.
l3: The set-out depends on the roof configuration and the information applicable to the construction.
l4: An experienced practitioner checks whether the set-out is consistent before errors are repeated across later roof framing work.
l5: Roof framing set-out follows relevant supporting construction and informs subsequent roof framing installation.

title: Under-slab drainage inspection
l1: Under-slab drainage includes drainage work that will become difficult to access after the slab is constructed.
l2: The relevant drainage work is checked before it becomes concealed by subsequent slab construction.
l3: The checks depend on the drainage work present and the stage at which it will become inaccessible.
l4: An experienced practitioner focuses on work that cannot be easily corrected once concrete has been placed.
l5: The inspection occurs after the relevant drainage work is installed and before slab construction conceals it.

title: Wet-area wall framing consideration
l1: Wall framing in a wet-area context may have requirements influenced by the construction and finishes associated with that area.
l2: The framing arrangement is checked against the relevant design and construction requirements before later finishes are installed.
l3: The appropriate framing arrangement can change depending on the wall system, finishes and project requirements.
l4: An experienced practitioner considers how later wet-area construction will interact with the framing rather than treating the frame in isolation.
l5: Wet-area framing decisions connect framing work with later lining, waterproofing and finishing activities.

title: Construction sequencing and concealment
l1: Construction sequencing determines the order in which related activities are carried out.
l2: Work is planned so that required inspections and checks occur before later activities conceal or restrict access to earlier work.
l3: The sequence can change when dependencies, access requirements or construction conditions change.
l4: An experienced practitioner looks ahead to identify work that will become inaccessible if the next activity proceeds.
l5: Sequencing connects preceding work, inspections, concealment points and downstream construction activities.

title: Wall frame set-out
l1: Wall frame set-out establishes the intended position of wall framing before the frame is completed.
l2: Wall positions are established from the relevant project information and checked before framing proceeds.
l3: Set-out decisions depend on the building layout and information applicable to the particular wall.
l4: An experienced practitioner checks the relationship between the wall position and surrounding construction before errors become difficult to correct.
l5: Wall frame set-out depends on earlier building layout information and informs subsequent framing activities.

title: Evidence before work is concealed
l1: Evidence of completed work provides a record that relevant construction was checked before it became concealed.
l2: Required evidence is captured at the appropriate stage before subsequent construction prevents normal observation of the work.
l3: The evidence required depends on the activity, inspection requirements and the type of work being concealed.
l4: An experienced practitioner recognises the last practical opportunity to inspect or record work before access is lost.
l5: Evidence collection is linked to inspection, concealment points and later verification of completed construction.

title: Construction decision dependencies
l1: A construction decision can depend on earlier work, available information and other related decisions.
l2: Dependencies are identified before making a decision so that relevant preceding conditions and downstream effects can be considered.
l3: The importance of a dependency changes according to the construction context and the decision being made.
l4: An experienced practitioner considers not only the immediate decision but also what has to happen before it and what it will affect afterwards.
l5: Decision dependencies connect related Knowledge Objects through preceding, following and dependency relationships.

title: Stud spacing and layout checks
l1: Stud spacing is a framing layout decision that must be checked against the applicable design.
l2: Review the framing layout information and identify the specified spacing before installation.
l3: Spacing decisions vary with the wall system, design and project documentation.
l4: A reviewer checks for consistency between framing layout and the information used by following trades.
l5: Stud layout follows wall set-out and influences later lining and service coordination.

title: Load path continuity at wall top plates
l1: Load-path continuity concerns how structural actions are transferred between connected building elements.
l2: Identify the relevant design details and review top-plate and blocking interfaces before concealment.
l3: Connection requirements depend on the engineered design and framing configuration.
l4: An experienced reviewer avoids treating a connection detail as interchangeable across different structural arrangements.
l5: Top-plate decisions relate to wall framing, roof framing and later inspections.

title: Under-slab drainage testing readiness
l1: Drainage testing is a verification activity before concealed plumbing becomes difficult to access.
l2: Confirm that the required testing and records are completed before proceeding to concealment.
l3: Testing methods and acceptance requirements depend on applicable specifications and licensed trade responsibilities.
l4: A reviewer checks that the test evidence corresponds to the installed work.
l5: Drainage installation and verification precede slab concealment.

title: Sanitary drain route coordination
l1: Sanitary drainage routing must be coordinated with the building layout and other services.
l2: Review planned routes and potential clashes with relevant trades before work is covered.
l3: Route choices depend on design, levels, access and site conditions.
l4: Experienced coordinators flag clashes early rather than relying on later rework.
l5: Drain routing informs excavation, slab preparation and future service access.

title: Site induction and work readiness
l1: Site induction communicates relevant site rules, hazards and responsibilities before work starts.
l2: Confirm that workers receive applicable induction information and know the escalation process.
l3: Induction content depends on the site and current work activities.
l4: A supervisor checks understanding rather than assuming attendance alone is enough.
l5: Induction precedes site work and links to ongoing hazard communication.

title: Escalating safety-critical concerns
l1: Safety-critical concerns require prompt escalation through the appropriate site process.
l2: Identify the concern, pause affected activity where required and refer it to authorised personnel.
l3: The response depends on the hazard, authority and applicable site procedures.
l4: Experienced supervisors avoid dismissing a serious concern solely because it disrupts the schedule.
l5: Safety escalation can interrupt planned sequencing until the issue is resolved.

title: Plant and pedestrian interface planning
l1: Mobile plant and pedestrian movements create an interface that requires active site planning.
l2: Review access routes, work zones and communication arrangements before overlapping activities.
l3: Controls depend on the equipment, space and site conditions.
l4: A supervisor watches for changes in movements that invalidate an earlier plan.
l5: Movement planning links deliveries, site access and work sequencing.

title: Unexpected excavation hazards
l1: Unexpected ground or excavation conditions can invalidate earlier work assumptions.
l2: Escalate the changed condition for appropriate assessment before affected work continues.
l3: Required actions depend on the nature of the discovery and site controls.
l4: Experienced practitioners recognise when an unforeseen condition exceeds the original work plan.
l5: Excavation decisions affect underground services and subsequent foundation work.

title: Roof catchment and drainage coordination
l1: Roof drainage planning considers how roof catchments relate to collection and discharge systems.
l2: Review the relevant design and coordination information before installing connected components.
l3: Sizing and configuration depend on project-specific design and applicable requirements.
l4: A reviewer checks that connected components are considered as a system.
l5: Catchment decisions inform gutters, downpipes and stormwater connections.

title: Roof drainage overflow provision
l1: Overflow provision is part of roof drainage risk management.
l2: Confirm that the documented overflow approach is coordinated with the roof drainage design.
l3: Requirements depend on the roof configuration and applicable design criteria.
l4: Experienced reviewers consider what happens when the primary drainage path is restricted.
l5: Overflow provision relates to catchment design, gutter arrangement and downstream drainage.

title: Gutter fall and drainage direction
l1: Gutter fall concerns the intended direction of water movement toward collection points.
l2: Check the installation against the documented drainage layout before handover.
l3: Required falls and detailing depend on the approved design and product system.
l4: A reviewer looks for inconsistencies between the planned outlet locations and installed arrangement.
l5: Gutter installation follows roof drainage set-out and connects to downpipes.

title: Preventing roof-sheet damage during adjacent work
l1: Adjacent construction activities can damage installed roof finishes.
l2: Coordinate work areas and inspect affected finishes after potentially damaging activities.
l3: The risk depends on tools, materials and work location.
l4: Experienced practitioners consider downstream defects from seemingly unrelated trade activities.
l5: Roof protection links trade sequencing, inspections and defect management.

title: Internal lining pre-start readiness
l1: Lining readiness means prerequisite framing and service activities have reached the agreed inspection point.
l2: Confirm relevant prerequisites and required checks before lining begins.
l3: Readiness depends on the project sequence and lining system.
l4: An experienced coordinator avoids covering unresolved preceding work.
l5: Lining follows framing and service rough-in and creates a concealment point.

title: Ceiling lining installation sequence
l1: Ceiling lining is sequenced with preceding overhead work and access requirements.
l2: Review prerequisites and planned installation order before closing the ceiling.
l3: Sequence changes with the ceiling system and coordination needs.
l4: A reviewer checks whether later trades still need access above the lining.
l5: Ceiling lining depends on completed overhead work and relevant verification.

title: Wet-area substrate readiness
l1: Wet-area substrates must suit the intended finishing and waterproofing systems.
l2: Check that substrate requirements and interface details are confirmed before finishes proceed.
l3: Requirements depend on the specified system and wet-area design.
l4: An experienced reviewer flags interface issues before they are concealed by finishes.
l5: Substrate readiness links framing, lining, waterproofing and tiling.

title: Dust exposure and trade separation
l1: Dust-generating activities can affect other workers and occupied work zones.
l2: Coordinate activity timing and site controls with responsible personnel.
l3: Controls depend on materials, tasks and applicable safety procedures.
l4: Experienced supervisors consider exposure beyond the worker performing the task.
l5: Dust management influences trade scheduling and access restrictions.

title: Electrical layout coordination
l1: Electrical layout information identifies intended positions of electrical components and service routes.
l2: Confirm current design information and coordinate interfaces before rough-in.
l3: Layout decisions depend on room use, design and licensed electrical requirements.
l4: A reviewer checks for clashes with framing, joinery and other services.
l5: Electrical layout precedes rough-in and informs later lining and fit-off.

title: Electrical positions in wet areas
l1: Electrical placement in wet areas has additional design and compliance considerations.
l2: Refer the proposed layout to the approved design and responsible licensed professionals.
l3: Applicable constraints depend on the room configuration and current requirements.
l4: An experienced coordinator does not infer safe positions from general room layouts.
l5: Wet-area electrical decisions interface with waterproofing, fixtures and finishes.

title: Cable routes and framing penetrations
l1: Electrical cable routing must be coordinated with framing and other building systems.
l2: Review route information and structural interfaces with authorised trades before concealment.
l3: Permitted penetrations and routing depend on the design and applicable requirements.
l4: A reviewer escalates potential conflicts rather than assuming modifications are acceptable.
l5: Cable routing follows framing layout and precedes wall or ceiling lining.

title: Electrical rough-in evidence before lining
l1: Pre-lining evidence can record electrical rough-in locations before they become concealed.
l2: Coordinate the required inspection and record capture before lining closes access.
l3: Evidence requirements depend on the project and responsible trade.
l4: An experienced coordinator checks that records identify the correct locations and stage.
l5: Electrical rough-in verification precedes lining and supports later maintenance.

title: Electrical energisation readiness
l1: Energisation is a controlled stage requiring appropriate verification and authorisation.
l2: Confirm that responsible licensed personnel have completed the required readiness process.
l3: The checks and authority depend on the installation and applicable rules.
l4: An experienced coordinator avoids treating physical completion as proof of safe energisation.
l5: Energisation follows installation and verification and precedes operational handover.

title: Residential HVAC capacity design inputs
l1: HVAC capacity selection depends on building-specific design inputs rather than room area alone.
l2: Collect the required design information and refer sizing to the responsible qualified designer.
l3: Loads vary with envelope performance, occupancy, climate and equipment assumptions.
l4: Experienced reviewers question unsupported rules of thumb when inputs are missing.
l5: Capacity design informs equipment selection, duct planning and commissioning.

title: HVAC first-fix coordination
l1: HVAC first-fix readiness depends on coordinated service locations and access.
l2: Review the agreed service routes and prerequisite work before concealment.
l3: Requirements depend on the system layout and other installed services.
l4: A reviewer looks for conflicts with framing, electrical work and ceiling access.
l5: HVAC first-fix follows design coordination and precedes lining.

title: Supply and return air location coordination
l1: Supply and return air locations influence the intended distribution of conditioned air.
l2: Review locations against the approved HVAC layout and surrounding building elements.
l3: Location decisions depend on room use, system design and access constraints.
l4: Experienced coordinators flag obstructions and later fit-out conflicts early.
l5: Air outlet planning connects HVAC design with ceiling and interior layout.

title: Duct route and access planning
l1: Duct routes need coordination with structure, ceiling space and future access.
l2: Review routing and access needs with relevant trades before installation.
l3: Route feasibility depends on available space and the designed system.
l4: A reviewer avoids concealing access conflicts that would affect future serviceability.
l5: Duct routing follows HVAC design and informs ceiling and service coordination.
